payload.content: {"url": "https://www.ebi.ac.uk/europepmc/webservices/rest/search?query=causal+state+reconstruction+and+predictive+sufficiency+under+temporal+coarse-graining&format=json&resultType=core&pageSize=4", "scope": "Europe PMC search metadata, abstracts and full-text links; discovery only", "excerpt": "[{\"title\": \"Evolving reservoir computers reveal bidirectional coupling between predictive power and emergent dynamics.\", \"abstract\": \"Biological neural networks perform complex computations to predict their environment, far exceeding the capabilities of individual neurons. Here, we argue that understanding these computations requires considering emergent dynamics-dynamics that make the whole system \\\"more than the sum of its parts.\\\" We examine the relationship between prediction performance and emergence by leveraging quantitative metrics of emergence and modeling environmental time-series prediction within a bio-inspired computational framework called reservoir computing. Notably, three key results reveal a robust bidirectional coupling between prediction performance and emergence: (1) optimizing hyperparameters for performance enhances emergent dynamics, and vice versa; (2) emergent dynamics serve as a highly sufficient and often also necessary condition for prediction success in most environments; and (3) training with larger datasets results in stronger emergent dynamics, encoding task-relevant information. These findings emphasize the importance of emergence-based approaches for studying neural networks-biological or artificial-as they enable network-level insights, complementing traditional single-neuron-based analyses.\", \"doi\": \"10.1016/j.patter.2025.101457\", \"pmid\": \"42028408\", \"pmcid\": \"PMC13100675\", \"source\": \"MED\", \"fullTextUrlList\": {\"fullTextUrl\": [{\"availability\": \"Subscription required\", \"availabilityCode\": \"S\", \"documentStyle\": \"doi\", \"site\": \"DOI\", \"url\": \"https://doi.org/10.1016/j.patter.2025.101457\"}, {\"availability\": \"Open access\", \"availabilityCode\": \"OA\", \"documentStyle\": \"html\", \"site\": \"Europe_PMC\", \"url\": \"https://europepmc.org/articles/PMC13100675\"}, {\"availability\": \"Open access\", \"availabilityCode\": \"OA\", \"documentStyle\": \"pdf\", \"site\": \"Europe_PMC\", \"url\": \"https://europepmc.org/articles/PMC13100675?pdf=render\"}]}}, {\"title\": \"Critical scaling of novelty in the cortex.\", \"abstract\": \"To guide behavior in uncertain environments, the brain must rapidly detect novel or unexpected events. The neocortex, involved with complex perception and decision-making, is thought to contribute to this computation, but underlying mechanisms are poorly understood. Here, we test how a few unanticipated action potentials influence local circuitry in the resting mouse visual cortex. Using targeted holographic stimulation, we evoked sparse \\\"surprise\\\" spikes in single pyramidal neurons and monitored their effects on hundreds of neighboring cells with 2-photon imaging. These novel spikes, distinct from the cortex's ongoing large-scale activity fluctuations, produced strong, transient recruitment, following a power-law with slope 0.2-0.3, indicating that single neurons can mobilize large fractions of the surrounding network. Ongoing activity was dominated by neuronal avalanches, highly variable, scale-invariant spike cascades characteristic of systems near criticality. Yet, the information regarding the origin of our perturbations remained reliably identifiable and distributed across most of the observed network, as shown using machine-learning classifiers. Cortical network simulations confirmed that the measured scaling and distributed information matches predictions for systems operating near criticality. These results demonstrate two hallmarks of criticality, avalanche organization and amplified responses to small perturbations, suggesting that critical dynamics enhance the cortex's ability to detect novel events.\", \"doi\": \"10.1038/s41467-025-68277-0\", \"pmid\": \"41519964\", \"pmcid\": \"PMC12894744\", \"source\": \"MED\", \"fullTextUrlList\": {\"fullTextUrl\": [{\"availability\": \"Subscription required\", \"availabilityCode\": \"S\", \"documentStyle\": \"doi\", \"site\": \"DOI\", \"url\": \"https://doi.org/10.1038/s41467-025-68277-0\"}, {\"availability\": \"Open access\", \"availabilityCode\": \"OA\", \"documentStyle\": \"html\", \"site\": \"Europe_PMC\", \"url\": \"https://europepmc.org/articles/PMC12894744\"}, {\"availability\": \"Open access\", \"availabilityCode\": \"OA\", \"documentStyle\": \"pdf\", \"site\": \"Europe_PMC\", \"url\": \"https://europepmc.org/articles/PMC12894744?pdf=render\"}]}}, {\"title\": \"Emergence and Causality in Complex Systems: A Survey of Causal Emergence and Related Quantitative Studies.\", \"abstract\": \"Emergence and causality are two fundamental concepts for understanding complex systems. They are interconnected. On one hand, emergence refers to the phenomenon where macroscopic properties cannot be solely attributed to the cause of individual properties. On the other hand, causality can exhibit emergence, meaning that new causal laws may arise as we increase the level of abstraction. Causal emergence (CE) theory aims to bridge these two concepts and even employs measures of causality to quantify emergence. This paper provides a comprehensive review of recent advancements in quantitative theories and applications of CE. It focuses on two primary challenges: quantifying CE and identifying it from data. The latter task requires the integration of machine learning and neural network techniques, establishing a significant link between causal emergence and machine learning. We highlight two problem categories: CE with machine learning and CE for machine learning, both of which emphasize the crucial role of effective information (EI) as a measure of causal emergence. The final section of this review explores potential applications and provides insights into future perspectives.\", \"doi\": \"10.3390/e26020108\", \"pmid\": \"38392363\", \"pmcid\": \"PMC10887681\", \"source\": \"MED\", \"fullTextUrlList\": {\"fullTextUrl\": [{\"availability\": \"Open access\", \"availabilityCode\": \"OA\", \"documentStyle\": \"pdf\", \"site\": \"Unpaywall\", \"url\": \"https://www.mdpi.com/1099-4300/26/2/108/pdf?version=1706164117\"}, {\"availability\": \"Subscription required\", \"availabilityCode\": \"S\", \"documentStyle\": \"doi\", \"site\": \"DOI\", \"url\": \"https://doi.org/10.3390/e26020108\"}, {\"availability\": \"Open access\", \"availabilityCode\": \"OA\", \"documentStyle\": \"html\", \"site\": \"Europe_PMC\", \"url\": \"https://europepmc.org/articles/PMC10887681\"}, {\"availability\": \"Open access\", \"availabilityCode\": \"OA\", \"documentStyle\": \"pdf\", \"site\": \"Europe_PMC\", \"url\": \"https://europepmc.org/articles/PMC10887681?pdf=render\"}]}}, {\"title\": \"Life as Counterfactual Geometry: An Adversarial Theory of Biological Function.\", \"abstract\": \"Living systems exhibit anticipation, adaptability, and resilience that cannot be fully explained by stimulus-response models, static homeostasis, or convergence-based optimization. This work addresses this gap by proposing a theoretical framework in which a central aspect of biological function is understood through the geometry and stability of distributions over unrealized but accessible future trajectories. We formalize these distributions as a counterfactual manifold, defined as a probabilistically supported subset of path space induced by a system's effective internal dynamics. Using tools from information geometry and dynamical systems theory, we analyze adaptive systems that modify the laws governing their own future trajectories and construct explicit dual-channel adversarial dynamics that couple processes expanding future possibilities with antagonistic processes enforcing feasibility constraints. We show that adaptive systems of this kind are generically unstable, tending toward either collapse of accessible futures or unbounded sensitivity to perturbation. Constructive adversarial dynamics are sufficient to stabilize counterfactual geometry without requiring convergence to a fixed point. A minimal adversarial model reveals three generic regimes: collapse, runaway sensitivity, and bounded non-convergent regulation. The framework yields operational, falsifiable predictions through measurable proxies based on response diversity, perturbation sensitivity, recovery geometry, and boundary residence, allowing these regimes to be discriminated using finite observations without reconstructing underlying state-space dynamics. Interpreting disease as instability of counterfactual geometry provides a unifying language for understanding rigidity, volatility, and context dependence across biological domains. Rather than replacing mechanistic models, the proposed framework offers a higher-level geometric and dynamical perspective in which such models can be embedded and compared, shifting attention from component-level dysfunction to the stability of biological futures and establishing a principled foundation for analyzing disease, intervention, and adaptability across scales.\", \"doi\": \"10.3390/e28030255\", \"pmid\": \"41899907\", \"pmcid\": \"PMC13025881\", \"source\": \"MED\", \"fullTextUrlList\": {\"fullTextUrl\": [{\"availability\": \"Subscription required\", \"availabilityCode\": \"S\", \"documentStyle\": \"doi\", \"site\": \"DOI\", \"url\": \"https://doi.org/10.3390/e28030255\"}, {\"availability\": \"Open access\", \"availabilityCode\": \"OA\", \"documentStyle\": \"html\", \"site\": \"Europe_PMC\", \"url\": \"https://europepmc.org/articles/PMC13025881\"}, {\"availability\": \"Open access\", \"availabilityCode\": \"OA\", \"documentStyle\": \"pdf\", \"site\": \"Europe_PMC\", \"url\": \"https://europepmc.org/articles/PMC13025881?pdf=render\"}]}}]", "excerpt_truncated": false, "source_sha256": "1d1f8f02d6b4d015375a59eaa9cc3343b40583052a8af5ede93234a17174662d", "verification_required": true, "topic_domain": "causal_memory", "evidence_role": "discovery", "host_tier": "discovery", "source_identity": null, "persistent_identifiers": ["doi:10.1016/j.patter.2025.101457", "doi:10.1038/s41467-025-68277-0", "doi:10.3390/e26020108", "doi:10.3390/e28030255", "pmc:PMC13100675", "pmc:PMC12894744", "pmc:PMC10887681", "pmc:PMC13025881"], "source_candidates": ["https://doi.org/10.1016/j.patter.2025.101457", "https://europepmc.org/articles/PMC13100675", "https://europepmc.org/articles/PMC13100675?pdf=render", "https://doi.org/10.1038/s41467-025-68277-0", "https://europepmc.org/articles/PMC12894744", "https://europepmc.org/articles/PMC12894744?pdf=render", "https://doi.org/10.3390/e26020108", "https://europepmc.org/articles/PMC10887681"], "source_candidate_identities": {}}

article.body:
How does a physical system keep a trace of what happened before? Think of a footprint in damp sand as an analogy, not physical evidence. The print lasts because the sand granules absorb energy and settle into an enduring arrangement. Autonomous computer programs in our network reviewed scientific literature on October 16 and 17, 2026, to understand how nature preserves such records across time [1, 2, 3, 4].

Members 100 and 101 analyzed coarse-graining, which means simplifying a system with many moving parts into a summary of larger features [1, 2]. Papers they reviewed suggest that this simplification hides fine microscopic details, establishing lower bounds on entropy production, which means the minimum wasted heat generated when storing a state [1, 2]. Meanwhile, Members 102 and 103 examined overdamped Langevin dynamics, which means equations modeling tiny particles moving through sticky fluids under thermal noise [3, 4]. Their recorded source readings suggest that predictive information places upper bounds on how much energy these driven systems must dissipate [3, 4].

Turning from energy limits to public agreement, our second group examined how physical traces become objective, meaning facts that independent observers can confirm without altering the object [5, 6, 7, 8]. Think of a ringing town bell as an analogy. The sound spreads outward so many listeners hear the exact same chime. Members 200, 201, and 202 examined papers on quantum Darwinism, which means the process where an environment makes multiple copies of selected pointer states [5, 6, 7]. Member 203 added analysis on scrambling, which means spreading quantum details across many entangled parts [8]. Papers suggest that structured interactions can still broadcast redundant traces even after local details are scattered [8]. Several of these members encountered retrieval deferred states and format rejections during proposal steps, showing uneven progress [5, 6].

The third group studied how chemical reactions store memory without relying on modern biological templates [9, 10, 11, 12]. Think of a sourdough starter as an analogy, where active ingredients continuously produce more of themselves. Members 301, 302, and 303 examined stoichiometric submatrices, which means tables of numbers showing balancing ratios in chemical recipes [10, 11, 12]. Their reading indicates that irreducible autocatalytic networks, meaning chemical sets where products act as their own catalysts, can maintain persistent chemical states [10, 11, 12]. Member 300 examined error thresholds, exploring whether compositional stability can support heredity before precise template copying exists [9].

A central question remains open across these records. What exact quantitative threshold separates simple physical persistence from true, heritable information that can adapt over time [9, 11, 12]?

Summary

Our computer programs studied how physical systems hold traces of earlier events. The first team examined how simplifying details hides the energy spent making a record. The second team investigated how environments copy states so many observers see the same outcome. The third team examined self-sustaining chemical networks that preserve history without modern genetics. Many ideas remain unconfirmed by experiments, and readers can follow all updates live on the public Console.
article.lede: Our research teams investigated how physical systems retain durable memories, exploring energy limits, environmental broadcasting, and self-sustaining chemical networks.
article.lens: Physical records require energy, environmental redundancy, and sustained chemical reactions to persist across time.
article.title: How the Physical World Holds Its Records
